title: How would you reduce a JavaScript bundle that has grown too large?
description: Learn a systematic approach to bundle size reduction: measure first, split aggressively, and verify with real production data.

data.text: Bundle bloat creeps in. A new library for date handling, a chart library for one dashboard, an icon set imported wholesale. The initial payload climbs past 300KB, then 500KB, and suddenly Lighthouse TTI is red and mobile users bounce. The answer is not 'use a smaller framework'—it's a systematic process: measure, split, tree-shake, lazy-load, and verify.

Use `webpack-bundle-analyzer` or `rollup-plugin-visualizer` to produce a treemap of your bundle. Look for three things: (1) a single massive dependency, (2) duplicate modules, and (3) modules you didn't expect to be there. The treemap tells you where the bytes live—without it, you're optimizing blind.

data.title: Analyze with webpack-bundle-analyzer
data.content: Add the plugin to your Next.js config to generate an interactive treemap of the client bundle.

terms.definition: Eliminating unused code from the final bundle during the build. Requires ES modules (`import`/`export`) and side-effect-free packages.
Dividing the bundle into smaller chunks loaded on demand, typically via dynamic `import()` or route-based splitting.
A separate JavaScript file produced by the bundler. Multiple chunks can be loaded in parallel.
Code that runs at import time (polyfills, global CSS injection). Marked in `package.json` `sideEffects` to tell the bundler not to tree-shake it.

data.text: Route-based splitting is the highest-impact change with the lowest risk. Next.js does this automatically, but if you're on a custom setup, configure your bundler to emit one chunk per route. Users only download the JS for the page they visit.

Components that are expensive to import or render—charts, rich text editors, map libraries—should be loaded only when needed. In Next.js, use `next/dynamic`. In a custom React app, use `React.lazy` with `Suspense`.

data.title: Dynamic import in Next.js
data.content: `next/dynamic` wraps a dynamic import and handles the loading state.

data.text: Run `npx next-bundle-analyzer` or `npx source-map-explorer` to find the biggest packages. For each large dependency, ask: do I need the whole library? Can I replace it with a smaller alternative? Common wins: replace `moment` with `date-fns` or `dayjs`, replace `lodash` with `lodash-es` and import only the functions you use.

data.title: Avoid importing entire lodash
data.content: Importing the full lodash pulls in every utility function. Import only what you need from the ES module build.

data.title: Tree-shaking requirements
data.text: Tree-shaking only works when the package uses ES modules (`export` syntax, not `module.exports`) and marks no side effects in `package.json`. Many older packages still ship CommonJS. Check if there's an ESM alternative or a modern drop-in like `lodash-es`.

items.text: Run bundle analyzer and identify the top 5 largest dependencies
items.hint: Look for libraries you only use in one place

items.text: Replace monolithic imports with named or per-function imports
Lazy-load route-level and below-fold components with `next/dynamic` or `React.lazy`
items.hint: Charts, editors, modals, and heavy third-party UI

items.text: Enable gzip or Brotli compression on the server
items.hint: Text-based assets like JS compress 70-80% with Brotli

items.text: Set `sideEffects: false` in your own package.json if applicable
items.hint: Tells Webpack it can safely tree-shake unused exports

items.question: Does dynamic import increase the number of HTTP requests?
items.answer: Yes, each dynamic import creates a new chunk. HTTP/2 multiplexes requests efficiently, so the overhead is low. For HTTP/1.1 or poor networks, balance chunk count against chunk size. Next.js groups dynamic imports intelligently.

items.question: What about bundle size vs total blocking time?
items.answer: Bundle size affects TTI and TBT because the parser must download and compile JS. But a large bundle that's loaded lazily doesn't block the initial render. Focus on the initial bundle first, then optimize above-the-fold chunks.

items.question: How do I prevent a library from being bundled at all?
items.answer: Use `externals` in Webpack or mark it as external in your bundler config. The library loads from a CDN instead. This is common for React, ReactDOM, and analytics scripts in production.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Measure with a bundle analyzer before making any changes
Route-based splitting gives the biggest win with the least risk
Lazy-load heavy components below the fold or off the critical path
Replace monolithic imports (e.g., full lodash) with per-function ESM imports
Verify with real production data—Lighthouse and CrUX, not just local dev
data.takeaway: Bundle optimization is a measurement-driven process. Splitting and tree-shaking, not framework switching, solve bloat.
